sources.citation: Lynch, John, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley. 2002. The Oceanic Languages. Richmond: Curzon.
sources.note: No Kapingamarangi sketch; Kapingamarangi appears only in the classification (Ellicean Outlier / Northwestern Outlier) and the typological-overview source table ('Kapingamarangi [Lieber 1974]'). Stress is discussed only for Oceanic in general ('Stress is generally fully predictable, falling on the penultimate syllable of a word', ch. 3, and POc penultimate stress, §3.1.4); no language-specific statement.

sources.note: Mentions Kapingamarangi only for syncope of 'unstressed vowels.. between identical consonants, giving rise to surface aspirates' (citing Milner 1958) and CV-reduplication with syncope (ppiki, ttuki, llaka); no statement of stress placement.

sources.citation: Lieber, Michael D. & Kalio H. Dikepa. 1974. Kapingamarangi Lexicon. PALI Language Texts: Polynesia. Honolulu: University Press of Hawaii. Open Access edition 2019 (PDF ISBN 9780824881320), 1044 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Intro §2 'The Kapingamarangi Orthography' (pp. xviii–xxi) covers only short/long vowels (10 vowels) and short/long consonants (18 consonants); §7 stem morphology describes reduplication by syllable shape (V/CV vs VV/CVV) without reference to stress; Appendix 1 'Phonetic Description of Kapingamarangi Orthographic Symbols' (pp. 971–972) lists segment articulations and vowel length only. Whole-text search for stress/accent/prominence/loud/emphatic yields no suprasegmental statement (only 'ancestress', 'speak loudly', 'EMPHATIC FORM' of pronouns).

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Kapingamarangi language' (phonology section derived from Lieber & Dikepa 1974: xvi–xvii and Elbert 1946)
sources.note: Consonants (18, plain vs aspirated/long), 10 vowels, diphthongs, syllable shapes VV/VVV/VCV/CVV/CCVV/CVCV/CCVCV; no statement about stress.

sources.citation: Elbert, Samuel H. 1948. Grammar and comparative study of the language of Kapingamarangi, texts, and word lists. Mimeographed final report to the Pacific Science Board, National Research Council (CIMA), 289 pp. (Glottolog: Elbert 1950, grammar sketch)

sources.note: The only grammar of the language in Glottolog's descriptive bibliography; a 289-page grammar with texts is the most likely place for an explicit stress statement, and it is the direct predecessor of Lieber & Dikepa's orthography.

tone.quote: Stress generally occurs according to the following rules. Stress is not indicated in phonemic transcription when it conforms to these rules: (1) All syllables containing long vowels or diphthongs (henceforth called LONG SYLLABLES) are stressed regardless of position. [...] (2) The penult and alternating preceding syllables are stressed, but long syllables are ignored in determining 'penult' and 'alternating preceding syllables', as in Ka-pi-nga-ma-ra-ngi.
tone.locator: p. 9, Part I Grammar, Phonemes, section 'Stress' (rules continue on p. 10 with (3) short unstressed monosyllables as separate words and (4) irregular stresses marked /'/); phoneme Summary with /'/ on p. 5
tone.n_tones: None: no tone described (prosodic phoneme inventory = stress /'/ only)
